**United States v. Negrete**
Late at night, a police officer in Des Moines, Iowa, stopped a vehicle because its registered owner had an outstanding warrant. David Negrete was the front-seat passenger. The officer detected a strong smell of marijuana and noted Negrete's suspicious behavior, such as shielding his face and looking down. After further suspicious movements by Negrete, an officer conducted a frisk, during which methamphetamine was found in Negrete’s pocket.
A firearm was also discovered under the seat where Negrete had been sitting and a backpack containing additional drugs and paraphernalia was located on the passenger side floor.Negrete was indicted for being a felon in possession of a firearm. He moved to suppress evidence obtained from his person and the vehicle, arguing that the detention and frisk were unlawful.
The United States District Court for the Southern District of Iowa denied the motion, finding the stop and detention lawful and the frisk constitutional except for an inadvertent intrusion into Negrete’s pocket, which yielded no evidence. UNITED STATES v. TURNER (2021) | FindLaw

 United States Court of Appeals, Eighth Circuit. UNITED STATES of America, Plaintiff - Appellee, v. Shawn David TURNER, Defendant - Appellant.

  Turner argues that the court erred in finding that he obstructed justice. A district court must apply a two-level increase if it finds that a defendant has “willfully obstructed or impeded ․ the administration of justice,” USSG § 3C1.1, as by “committing ․ perjury” or “providing materially false information to a judge.” Id., comment. (n.4(B), (F)). A witness commits perjury if he “gives false testimony concerning a material matter with the willful intent to provide false testimony” while under oath. United States v. Dunnigan, 507 U.S. 87, 94, 113 S.Ct. 1111, 122 L.Ed.2d 445 (1993). “Lying to obtain a lighter sentence” is obstruction of justice under § 3C1.1. United States v. Moore, 624 F.3d 875, 878 (8th Cir. 2010). The standard of proof is a preponderance of the evidence, United States v. Negrete, 537 F.3d 918, 922 (8th Cir. 2008), and we review the district court's findings for clear error. United States v. Sanders, 956 F.3d 534, 540 (8th Cir. 2020).

  Turner also contends that his sentence is substantively unreasonable. He argues that the court gave too little weight to his history of addiction, his remorse and rehabilitation, and the deterrent effect of a shorter sentence. We review the substantive reasonableness of a sentence for abuse of discretion. United States v. Feemster, 572 F.3d 455, 461 (8th Cir. 2009) (en banc). A court abuses its discretion if it “commits a clear error of judgment” in weighing the factors in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a). Id. (quoting United States v. Kane, 552 F.3d 748, 752 (8th Cir. 2009)).

# UNITED STATES v. NEGRETE (2026)
## United States Court of Appeals, Eighth Circuit.
###
UNITED STATES of America, Plaintiff - Appellee v. David Lee NEGRETE, Defendant - Appellant
### No. 25-3409
### Decided: October 08, 2026

David Negrete pled guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm under 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1) and 924(a)(8), and the district court 1 sentenced him to 77 months of imprisonment. Before pleading guilty, Negrete moved to suppress evidence obtained during a search of his person and a vehicle in which he was a passenger. Negrete appeals the denial of his motion to suppress and the sentence. We affirm.
I. Background
Shortly after midnight, Des Moines, Iowa, Police Officer Matthew Sander stopped a vehicle because its registered owner had an outstanding warrant. After requesting backup, he approached the vehicle and saw two occupants in the vehicle's front seats. The passenger, David Negrete, rolled down the window, and Officer Sander detected a strong odor of marijuana. While speaking to the vehicle's owner, Officer Sander noticed Negrete was shielding his face from view and looking down.

A grand jury indicted Negrete under 18 U.S.C. §§ 922(g)(1) and 924(a)(8) for possessing a firearm as a convicted felon, and Negrete moved to suppress evidence seized from his person and the vehicle. The district court denied his motion. Negrete entered a conditional guilty plea, which preserved his right to appeal the denial of his suppression motion. At sentencing, the district court found that, because “the gun was loaded and right underneath the seat where Mr. Negrete was sitting,” the firearm had the potential to facilitate the possession of drugs. The court therefore applied a four-level enhancement for possessing a firearm in connection with another felony offense and sentenced him to 77 months of imprisonment, the bottom of the applicable Guidelines range. Negrete timely appealed.

During the frisk, an officer mistakenly placed his hand inside Negrete’s left pants pocket but immediately withdrew it without finding evidence. The officer then felt suspected contraband through Negrete’s right pants pocket and later removed methamphetamine. A vehicle search uncovered a loaded firearm beneath Negrete’s seat and a backpack containing controlled substances and drug paraphernalia. Negrete conditionally pleaded guilty to being a felon in possession of a firearm, preserving his suppression challenge, and received a 77-month sentence after the district court applied a four-level enhancement for possessing the firearm in connection with another felony offense.

The Eighth Circuit affirmed the denial of suppression. It held that Negrete’s detention was lawful because the vehicle stop was supported by the owner’s outstanding warrant, and ordering Negrete to reenter and remain in the vehicle while officers arrested the driver was a reasonable safety measure under the circumstances.

The court agreed that the officer exceeded the permissible scope of a Terry frisk by reaching inside Negrete’s left pants pocket. Suppression was unwarranted, however, because that intrusion yielded no evidence and was not a but-for cause of discovering the methamphetamine in the right pocket. The district court also did not clearly err in crediting the officer’s testimony that the contraband’s incriminating character was immediately apparent by touch, even though the officer completed the weapons frisk before retrieving it.

The court also upheld the four-level enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1 (b) (7) (B). The district court did not merely presume a connection between the gun and Negrete’s drug possession; it found that the loaded firearm directly beneath his seat had the potential to facilitate that offense. The record supported that finding because Negrete possessed drugs on his person while a loaded weapon was readily accessible nearby in the vehicle.
